item.title: New dinosaur fossil discovery fills gap in Early Cretaceous fossil record in Inner Mongolia, North China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 17:16:00
Fossil localities and specimen photographs Photo: Inner Mongolia Museum of Natural History Digital reconstruction of the dentary Photo: Inner Mongolia Museum of Natural History Chinese researchers have discovered the first Early Cretaceous hadrosauroid dinosaur fossil in the Erlian Basin in North China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. The study, published in the international paleontological journal Fossil Record, fills a gap in the region's fossil record and offers new clues to the early evolution and diversification of the herbivorous dinosaur group. The study, titled "The First Hadrosauroid Dinosaur from the Lower Cretaceous of the Erlian Basin, Inner Mongolia, China," was led by the Inner Mongolia Museum of Natural History, with participation from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Shenyang Normal University, among other institutions. Unearthed in Ejin Horo township, East Ujimqin banner, the fossil is the first recorded hadrosauroid specimen from the Lower Cretaceous strata of the Erlian Basin. The specimen is now housed at the Inner Mongolia Museum of Natural History, comprising a left dentary, teeth, vertebrae, toe bones and several bone fragments. Although fragmented and scattered, the bones were found concentrated in a relatively small area, suggesting that the specimen was buried close to its original position, according to preliminary assessments. Hadrosauroids were among the most abundant groups of herbivorous dinosaurs of the Cretaceous Period. Their earliest known fossils date back to the Early Cretaceous, and the group reached its peak diversity in the Late Cretaceous before spreading worldwide. Early Cretaceous hadrosauroid fossils have mainly been found in East Asia, including western Liaoning Province, Mazongshan in Gansu Province, the Alxa-Bayannur region of western Inner Mongolia and the eastern Gobi Desert in Mongolia. Most studies suggest that Asia was the center of origin and early diversification and dispersal of hadrosauroids. Located between these fossil-rich regions, the Erlian Basin had previously yielded no reported Early Cretaceous hadrosauroid fossils. The discovery has filled a gap in the fossil record between these localities, indicating that hadrosauroids were already inhabiting the basin during the Early Cretaceous. Researchers found that the new specimen exhibits a combination of primitive and more advanced traits. It retains primitive features of early ornithopod dinosaurs, such as accessory ridges on both the mesial and distal sides of the primary ridge on its upper jaw teeth. It also displays several features closer to those of hadrosaurids, including an elongated toothless region at the front of the dentary, more tooth positions and a primary ridge positioned near the center of the teeth. These traits provide important clues for reconstructing the early evolutionary sequence of key features in hadrosaurids and suggest that hadrosauroids had already developed considerable diversity during the Early Cretaceous. Despite the incomplete preservation of the specimen, its distinctive combination of morphological features suggests that it may represent a new genus and species of hadrosauroid outside the hadrosaurid family. More systematic field surveys and rescue excavations aimed at obtaining more complete fossil material will be essential for determining the specimen's exact taxonomic position and clarifying how key hadrosauroid traits evolved. The fossil was recovered through a rescue excavation conducted under a project commissioned by the department of natural resources of the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. In recent years, the Inner Mongolia Museum of Natural History has stepped up efforts to survey regional fossil resources, carry out rescue excavations, restore specimens, develop joint research platforms and promote public science education.

item.title: Narrowing economic 'temperature gap,' and keeping confidence intact
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 15:57:00
Robotic arms operate at high speed on the production line, with technicians rushing to complete orders for dual-clutch automatic transmissions at a plant in Changxing, East China's Zhejiang Province on February 23, 2026. Workers are back at the company after the Chinese Lunar New Year, with all production lines running at full capacity. Photo: VCG Since the start of this year, China's economy has moved ahead against headwinds, maintaining an overall stable trajectory, developing with new growth drivers and demonstrating strong resilience and vitality. To borrow the words of the spokesperson for the National Bureau of Statistics, "the characteristics of stability are pronounced, and the foundations for stability are stronger." This is evident in the data for the first 10 months, including foreign trade growth, value-added of industrial enterprises above the designated size, and strong growth in high-tech manufacturing. Yet compared with the macro data, many micro-level indicators display some "temperature gap". Monthly exports, for instance, grew by more than 30 percent nationwide, but many businesses complain that "business is getting harder" and that "cash flow is under strain." Likewise, many enterprises tied to new quality productive forces are expanding rapidly, while workers in some traditional industries are grappling with the growing pains of transition. In particular, although the overall economy is growing steadily, the way households perceive their income and the pace of consumption recovery do not move fully in lockstep. Taking this "temperature gap" seriously is not to deny the veracity of the macro data, but to understand more accurately the structural contradictions of an economy in transition, to clear the "last mile" in policy implementation, and to ensure that the dividends of growth are passed on more evenly to businesses and ordinary people. Objectively, the gap between the macro picture and individual experience today has different characteristics, if compared with previous years. In the past, such gaps mostly stemmed from external shocks and short-term disruptions, with the problems concentrated in clogged distribution and temporary shutdowns; many businesses expected that "once we get through this, things will return to the old track." Such anxiety carried a degree of uncertainty, but the underlying industrial layout and employment structure did not change fundamentally. People shop at the Haikou International Duty Free Shopping Complex in Haikou, south China's Hainan Province, July 18, 2026. (Xinhua/Yang Guanyu) Today's gap stems more from structural adjustment in the shift from the old to the new growth drivers. In the past, the engines of growth were spread broadly across traditional manufacturing and services, which absorbed a large workforce, so increments in growth easily flowed through to millions of households. Now, the core engines of growth are concentrated in high-tech manufacturing and the "new three" export categories — new quality productive forces — where the sectoral threshold is higher, and the chains through which industrial spillovers and job creation are transmitted are longer. In other words, groups in the new development tracks can enjoy the dividends of transition sooner, while most businesses in traditional tracks have yet to adapt to the pace of change, and the dividends of growth have not yet reached them fully. In practice, this shows up as orders growing without a direct rise in revenue and profit, benefits reaching upstream and downstream players more slowly than they reach those leading firms. To view this "temperature gap" rationally, we must neither ignore the real difficulties of micro-level actors simply because of impressive macro indicators and dismiss individual experiences as subjective judgments, nor deny that the overall economy is stabilizing and improving and that the shift from the old to new growth drivers is accelerating simply because some feel pressure. At present, the direction of China's industrial upgrading and opening-up has not changed, and the development of new quality productive forces is building more momentum for growth. But we must also recognize that the emergence of the "temperature gap" shows that blockages remain in the economic circulation, and it reminds us that policy must not focus only on aggregate indicators but must pay closer attention to micro-level experience, better aligning macro goals with individual expectations. Narrowing the "temperature gap" between the macro picture and individuals will not happen overnight. The key is to open up the transmission chain between the overall economy and micro-level actors and to make coordinated efforts on multiple fronts so that the dividends of development reach millions of households more effectively. Optimizing the industrial transmission mechanism is the precondition. We need to move faster to resolve the structural problem of new growth dividends being concentrated in leading firms, push orders and technology outward to supporting small and medium-sized enterprises, expand the reach of those who benefit from growth, and promote integrated development among large, medium and small enterprises. We need to straighten out the income distribution chain, open the channel through which output value and profit are converted into pay, improve the mechanism for reasonable wage growth, broaden channels for diversified income, and narrow income gaps between groups. Relieving the difficulties of small and micro businesses is the key. We need to move faster to lower transaction costs of all kinds, work to resolve the problem of accounts receivable, keep the channels for delivering pro-business policies open, and energize the economic capillaries that absorb employment. We must firmly uphold the priority of employment, balance job creation with support for livelihood-related services, strengthen vocational skills training, focus on safeguarding employment for key groups, and steadily enhance the sense of gain among working people. Stabilizing social expectations is the priority. We need to continue to build a broad social security net covering medical care and elderly care, guide social expectations sensibly, and build consensus around development. On the foundation of ensuring basic livelihoods, we should improve income distribution mechanisms, making the pie bigger while dividing it fairly, gradually closing the perceived gap, and achieving resonance between an expanding economy and improving livelihoods. This was compiled and translated by the Global Times English edition based on an article published on the Economic Daily on November 21, 2026.

item.title: Chinese, Vietnamese navies complete 41st joint patrol in Beibu Gulf to strengthen maritime security cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 12:44:00
Photo: PLA Navy The Chinese and Vietnamese navies have successfully completed their 41st joint patrol in the Beibu Gulf over two days, covering 351 nautical miles in 32 hours and including a joint maritime search-and-rescue drill, the PLA Daily reported on Sunday. During the joint patrol, China deployed the naval vessels Wuzhou and Enshi, while Vietnam sent two naval vessels to participate. The Chinese and Vietnamese vessels arrived in their designated patrol area in the Beibu Gulf on Friday. After establishing communications, the two sides patrolled in two parallel columns along the China-Vietnam demarcation line in the gulf. During the operation, the two sides transferred command authority in stages and exchanged data on courses, speeds and other operational details, maintaining real-time awareness of the maritime situation. On Saturday, the joint patrol fleet held a search-and-rescue drill simulating two fishing vessels in distress in the Beibu Gulf. After being informed that crew members had fallen overboard, the fleet adjusted its course and speed, drew up search-and-rescue plan and used multiple search methods to accurately locate and rescue the personnel in the water. After the exercise, the fleet practiced coordinated formation changes under agreed rules for alternating command, including single-column, single-line-abreast and double-column formations. Both sides maintained close communication and demonstrated smooth coordination throughout the drills. After completing all scheduled drills, the Chinese and Vietnamese vessels separated and departed in different directions. Personnel from both sides lined up in their respective areas and waved goodbye, marking the successful conclusion of the 41st China-Vietnam joint patrol. The PLA Daily cited a Chinese commander as saying that adding exercises to the joint patrol enhanced the two navies' ability to conduct coordinated operations and promoted professional exchanges and practical cooperation between the two sides. The China-Vietnam joint patrols in the Beibu Gulf are friendly exchanges conducted by the two militaries under relevant agreements and annual plans. The report said the patrols help strengthen friendship between the two countries, deepen mutual trust between their armed forces, and effectively enhancing both sides' ability to respond jointly to maritime emergencies and safeguard maritime security and stability. item.title: China opposes unwarranted US targeting of Chinese telecom companies: MOFCOM
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 10:11:00
The Ministry of Commerce of China File photo: VCG China firmly opposes the US Federal Communications Commission's (FCC) proposal to prohibit Chinese telecom operators from directly obtaining US internet telephone numbering resources, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) said on Sunday, noting that the FCC has abused its regulatory authority, generalized so-called national security risks, and, in the absence of factual basis, violated the principles of non-discrimination and fair competition by wantonly smearing and maliciously suppressing Chinese telecom enterprises operating in the US. The remarks came after the FCC recently voted to adopt a rule proposal that would bar telecom operators including China Telecom, China Unicom and China Mobile, which have been placed on the "Covered List" from directly obtaining US internet telephone numbering resources. The spokesperson noted that the US agency has recently continued to push for decoupling and severing ties between China and the US in the fields of telecommunications, communications, and testing and certification, according to a statement released on the MOFCOM's official website on Sunday. "These actions run counter to the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, undermine the stable bilateral economic and trade relationship, and China firmly opposes them." China urges the US to immediately revoke the relevant measures and return to the right path of resolving issues through consultations. China will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own interests, the MOFCOM spokesperson said. Chinese experts have criticized the FCC's move, saying it fundamentally undermines the principle of open and uninterrupted communications systems. Xiang Ligang, a veteran industry analyst, told the Global Times on Monday that the US' attempt to link China's telecom development with so-called security concerns reflects a tendency to politicize technological competition, which risks restricting market competition and undermining international cooperation. "The US gains nothing from these restrictions, while the broader impact is to disrupt global connectivity, hinder communication among countries, and damage international exchanges," Xiang said, adding that the move is "extremely negative" and harmful to world peace, as well as to human communication and development. Global Times

item.title: Guarding green rainforest in China's southernmost province
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 08:20:00
A drone photo taken on Sept. 10, 2026 shows a view of the Wuzhishan section of the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park in south China's Hainan Province. (Xinhua/Pu Xiaoxu) Early in the morning, the mountainous rainforest of Wuzhishan in south China's Hainan Province is still shrouded in thick clouds and mist. Wang Cheng opens the "Rainforest Patrol" application on his phone, gets on his motorcycle and sets off for his patrol mission through the mountains. As he travels, his route is automatically recorded on an electronic map. Wang's family has lived at the foot of these mountains for generations, and the 44-year-old ethnic Li forest ranger treats the forests of his hometown as old friends, deserving of constant care and protection. Decades ago, local villagers depended heavily on the mountains for their livelihoods. Logging and slash-and-burn farming had fragmented parts of the rainforest. In 2021, China established its first five national parks, including the National Park of Hainan Tropical Rainforest. Since then, protecting the rainforest has become a shared responsibility, extending beyond the work of government departments and researchers to local communities. Many villagers inside the park have transitioned into forest ranger roles, with Wang being one of them. This photo taken on Sept. 9, 2026 shows a stream at the Diaoluoshan section of the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park in south China's Hainan Province. (Xinhua/Pu Xiaoxu) The transformation of Hainan's rainforest is once again in the international spotlight as the province hosts the ongoing 2026 Tropical Rainforest Ecosystem Partners Conference. The event, underway in the provincial capital Haikou, has brought together international officials, experts and representatives from more than 20 countries to exchange views on rainforest conservation and sustainable development. Discussions have covered water conservation and ecological security, biodiversity protection, the development and utilization of forest food resources, mechanisms for realizing the value of ecological products, cultural heritage preservation and rainforest carbon governance. This photo taken on Nov. 19, 2026 shows a scene at the 2026 Tropical Rainforest Ecosystem Partners Conference in Haikou, south China's Hainan Province. (Xinhua/Yang Guanyu) International speakers at the conference highlighted the global importance of rainforest conservation, emphasizing its close links with food security, climate resilience and human well-being. A think tank report titled "A Great Song Resounds in the Rainforest: The 'Hainan Model' of China's Tropical Rainforest Conservation" was released at the event, examining Hainan's experience in protecting its tropical rainforest ecosystem. Hainan's tropical rainforest is the most concentrated, best-preserved and largest contiguous continental-island-type tropical rainforest in China, and forms an important part of the world's tropical rainforest system. Over the years, authorities have stepped up efforts to protect its valuable natural heritage. The results are increasingly visible on the ground. On his patrols, Wang often spots tree crabs, which are indicators of a healthy rainforest ecosystem. Infrared cameras also frequently capture images of rare birds and animals. Behind these observations is a "space-air-ground integrated" monitoring network operating within the park, combining satellite remote sensing, drones, acoustic monitoring devices and on-the-ground ranger patrols. "When I see these creatures living and thriving peacefully, I know this forest has truly come back to life," Wang said. The wildlife recovery reflects a whole set of systematic governance reforms. The National Park of Hainan Tropical Rainforest consolidated more than 20 previously scattered protected areas, relying on natural restoration supplemented by moderate artificial restoration to safeguard the rainforest's integrity. The province has also completed China's first natural-resource ownership registration for a national park, taking stock of its forests, wetlands and water resources. Authorities orderly completed the ecological relocation of 459 households totaling 1,975 people from the core protected zone of the park. Yet the challenges facing tropical rainforests extend far beyond Hainan. The ongoing strong El Niño phenomenon is pushing the world's tropical rainforests to the brink of crisis. Rising forest fire risks, disturbed wildlife habitats and disrupted ecological water cycles continue to plague many tropical countries, where the tension between ecological protection and livelihood development persists. "China's tropical rainforest management is already quite comprehensive," said Maria Rosda Lima Panggur, forest ecosystem manager at Komodo National Park in Indonesia, speaking at the conference. The report not only profiles the biodiversity information, but also includes the cultural heritage -- how local communities relate to nature -- as well as conservation management and a big part of technology, such as smart patrols and monitoring, according to her. "I think it's really a great effort for biodiversity conservation," she added. For Wang, however, the challenges of rainforest conservation are increasingly apparent. El Niño has brought prolonged high temperatures and drought, adding to the daily pressure of forest management. During his patrols, he must now keep an even closer watch for fire risks and closely monitor the effects of dry weather on the survival of plants and animals. "We guard the mountains, and the mountains guard us," he said.

item.title: Forum held to exchange poverty reduction experience, approaches between China, Africa
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-22 08:11:00
Xue Songyan, secretary-general of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, speaks at a high-level thematic forum on poverty reduction in Addis Ababa, the Ethiopian capital, Nov. 21, 2026. A high-level thematic forum was held on Saturday in Addis Ababa, the Ethiopian capital, to further deepen China-Africa cooperation on poverty reduction through enhanced exchanges of practical experience and development approaches. (Photo by Michael Tewelde/Xinhua) A high-level thematic forum was held on Saturday in Addis Ababa, the Ethiopian capital, to further deepen China-Africa cooperation on poverty reduction through enhanced exchanges of practical experience and development approaches. Held under the theme "China-Africa Exchange of Poverty Reduction Experience and Practical Approaches," the forum brought together representatives from China, Ethiopia, and other African countries to explore new avenues of cooperation and foster Sino-African institutional knowledge sharing in support of global poverty alleviation efforts. Experts and academicians at the forum called for translating shared development experience into practical, country-specific solutions while respecting each nation's independent path, noting that poverty is not destiny and can be overcome through targeted action, productive transformation, and sustained partnerships. Addressing the gathering, Xue Songyan, secretary-general of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS), noted that China has completed the largest poverty alleviation campaign in human history, realizing the United Nations poverty reduction goal 10 years ahead of schedule. Outlining five think tank priorities, Xue said CASS and the China-Africa Institute will advance academic exchanges, conduct joint field research, foster two-way communication on knowledge products, support talent cultivation through scholar exchanges, and strengthen linkages and cooperation with African think tanks. The forum emphasized greater alignment of Sino-African cooperation with national development strategies and local priorities, stressing that poverty reduction requires strong governance, institutional support, and active citizen participation. Tefera Derbew, former Ethiopian ambassador to China, noted that poverty is a multidimensional challenge affecting the dignity, stability, and potential of communities and nations. Ethiopia has pursued agricultural transformation, infrastructure expansion, human capital growth, environmental restoration, and economic reforms under its 10-year development plan and homegrown economic reform agenda to address structural constraints. Calling for enhanced cooperation across productive investments, technology transfer, and local capacity building, Derbew underscored the vital need to further deepen collaboration through country-specific programs aligned with national priorities that create jobs and help people permanently escape poverty. Participants stressed that poverty reduction should be integrated into broader economic and social development, combining infrastructure, agricultural improvement, education, and skills training to build long-term resilience rather than relying solely on temporary relief. For his part, Chinese Ambassador to Ethiopia Chen Hai described poverty as a common challenge facing humanity, and poverty reduction and development as issues bearing on the well-being of all humanity. As a large developing country, China has secured victory in the largest-scale poverty alleviation battle in human history, lifting nearly 100 million rural poor people out of poverty. China has eradicated absolute poverty across the board, fulfilling a millennium-old dream and century-long aspiration of the Chinese people, he said. Chen finally highlighted that China, pursuing the principles of sincerity, real results, amity, and good faith, stands ready to share poverty reduction concepts, experience, and approaches with partners in need, offering a useful reference for developing countries to independently explore their own paths to modernization, deliver mutual benefits and win-win outcomes, and inject new momentum into global poverty reduction efforts. item.title: 3.95-billion-year-old rock discovered in China, oldest known in Asia
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-21 20:49:00
The 3.95-billion-year-old granitic gneiss found in Lulong county, North China's Hebei Province. Recognized as Asia’s oldest known rock, it may offer fresh evidence for early Earth tectonic evolution. Photo: Screenshot from the CCTV News Chinese scientists have discovered a rock dating back 3.95 billion years in North China's Hebei Province, making it the oldest rock ever identified in Asia and offering a rare glimpse into Earth's infancy. The discovery was made in Lulong county, where the ancient rock, a type of granitic gneiss, is exposed over an area of just about 15 square meters – roughly the size of a small room, CCTV News learned from the China Geological Survey under the Ministry of Natural Resources. At approximately 3.95 billion years old, the rock dates back to a time when Earth was still in its infancy. The planet itself is estimated to be about 4.6 billion years old, meaning the newly identified specimen formed when Earth was only around 650 million years into its existence. Rocks from this early chapter of Earth's history are exceptionally rare. The oldest widely recognized rock formation previously known was the Acasta Gneiss in Canada, estimated to be about 4 billion years old. The Chinese discovery pushes back the age record for China's oldest known rocks by 150 million years, narrowing the gap with the world's oldest known rocks to around 50 million years. Scientists determined the rock's age by analyzing tiny zircon minerals embedded in it, which act as natural time capsules preserving a record of Earth's early history. But determining the rock's age was only the beginning. Further analysis of its chemical composition has yielded two additional findings that could shed new light on how early Earth evolved. First, the findings suggest that Earth may already have experienced tectonic processes resembling modern-day plate subduction as early as 3.95 billion years ago. In such processes, material from the Earth's surface is carried deep underground, potentially tens of kilometers below the surface. This would mean that such geological activity may have begun much earlier than previously thought. Second, the study suggests that large-scale differentiation between Earth's crust and mantle had already begun around 4.3 billion years ago, offering new evidence for reconstructing how the planet took shape in its earliest stages.

item.title: Anthropic rings the bell: Why were there no Chinese faces?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-21 00:07:00
File photo VCG On November 19, leading US AI company Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut in what was described as the largest IPO in history, with its market capitalization briefly climbing to nearly $2 trillion. However, among the seven founders who rang the opening bell at the ceremony, not a single Chinese face was present. Many netizens pointed out that while Chinese engineers had made indispensable contributions to Anthropic's growth, gaining access to its board and core decision-making circles remained extremely difficult. This has prompted questions about whether Chinese professionals being shut out of top decision-making positions is an unspoken "rule" in Silicon Valley. Chinese engineers are highly capable technically, but as a whole, they remain concentrated in frontline research and engineering roles, with limited opportunities to advance into the highest levels of corporate decision-making. This is a common problem among US technology companies. Data from US think tanks such as MacroPolo show that, at one point, Chinese researchers (based on undergraduate degrees) accounted for around 38 percent of top-tier AI researchers in the US. In some years, researchers from China even outnumbered those from the US among top-tier AI researchers worldwide. Chinese researchers and engineers are also well represented on the initial team at Meta's Superintelligence Labs and among key research contributors at OpenAI and Anthropic. The technological foundations of these companies rely heavily on Chinese engineers and researchers, while decision-making power remains largely in the hands of founding teams and established networks. There is even a specific term for this phenomenon: the "bamboo ceiling." The stark contrast between Silicon Valley's heavy reliance on Chinese technical talent and the limited representation of Chinese professionals in its top decision-making circles also undermines the Silicon Valley myth that technical excellence alone guarantees equal rewards. Leading technology companies and elite circles have long prided themselves on being "diverse and inclusive." Yet this inclusiveness is, to a considerable extent, reserved for the privileged. From the early days of the semiconductor industry to today's cutting-edge fields of large AI models, computing power and algorithms, numerous Chinese researchers have contributed their expertise. Yet they are often confined to the role of "technical contributors", rarely taking center stage at milestone moments such as IPO bell-ringing events or strategic decision-making forums - platforms that symbolize recognition and a voice in decision-making. This points to a long-standing structural barrier. In recent years, the environment for Chinese technology professionals in Western countries has deteriorated markedly. Prejudice once concealed beneath the rhetoric of "free movement of talent" has increasingly surfaced under the guise of "national security." This policy-level distrust, compounded by heightened scrutiny based on identity amid geopolitical tensions, has further narrowed opportunities for Chinese professionals to advance. In the wake of the controversy surrounding Jensen Huang, some Western media outlets have openly spread the false claim that "all Chinese are spies," fueling anti-China and anti-Chinese rhetoric. In such an atmosphere, Chinese professionals may still be automatically branded as "untrustworthy," no matter how impressive their professional achievements are. At the core of competition for talent is respect for and fair treatment of innovators. An advantage built on suspicion, barriers and exclusionary networks cannot last. Recently, news that Liu Jun, a member of the US National Academy of Sciences, had returned to China to take up a teaching position caused a stir in US public opinion. There is little reason to be surprised. Talent naturally gravitates toward places where the environment is more open, policies are more stable and support systems are more comprehensive. That is simply how the world works.

item.title: 'Thank You, China' from world leaders is more than just a courtesy: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-21 00:00:00
This photo taken on November 16, 2026 shows a view of Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province with APEC elements. China will hold the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen from November 18 to 19. Photo: VCG Behind the widely shared expressions of "Thank you, China" lies not only an expectation of further cooperation, but also a vote of confidence in China as a reliable partner. As the host, China patiently built bridges of communication, responding to major economies' concerns over industrial chain stability and technological innovation while listening to the pressing needs of developing members for infrastructure, capacity building and green transition. The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting has successfully concluded. Before heading home, leaders from various economies expressed their sincere gratitude to Chinese President Xi Jinping, China, the host of this meeting, and the city of Shenzhen. Russian President Vladimir Putin said he "congratulates" Chinese friends' hosting of a "very successful APEC summit." US President Donald Trump said that if the highest possible score were 10, he would give his visit to China "a 12." Leaders from Vietnam, South Korea, Malaysia, Thailand and Canada, as well as representatives of international organizations and other participants, also spoke highly of the achievements of China's APEC Year and expressed their appreciation for the excellent work of the Chinese side. It is hard to say goodbye after a visit to Shenzhen. The Shenzhen APEC meeting has left a distinctive mark on the history of APEC and a lasting impression on the hearts and minds of participating economies across the Asia-Pacific. During the Shenzhen meeting, leaders of various economies created many heartwarming moments as they stepped out of conference venues and into the city's streets. Beyond the meeting rooms, the streets of Shenzhen became places for unexpected encounters. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, whose ancestral roots trace back to Guangdong Province, showed off his Cantonese skills on several occasions. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese sampled beef at a supermarket, while Mexico's Secretary of Health David Kershenobich Stalnikowitz visited Huaqiangbei, a bustling commercial district popular with international visitors. These heartwarming moments not only became trending topics on Chinese social media, but also left fond memories for guests from various sides who had traveled from afar. Behind the widely shared expressions of "Thank you, China" lies not only an expectation of further cooperation, but also a vote of confidence in China as a reliable partner. At a time when protectionism is on the rise and global economic growth is under pressure, bringing 21 APEC member economies together around the same table is no easy task. This is all the more challenging given the vast differences in their economic size, stages of development and diverse interests. An equal platform for dialogue and in-depth discussion is therefore all the more necessary. As the host, China patiently built bridges of communication, responding to major economies' concerns over industrial chain stability and technological innovation while listening to the pressing needs of developing members in infrastructure, capacity building and green transition. Leaders from various economies consistently praised China's thoughtful and efficient organization, as well as the candid and pragmatic atmosphere for communication. The meeting also forged tangible consensus. From the Suzhou Statement at the APEC Ministers Responsible for Trade Meeting to the Chengdu Statement at the APEC Digital and AI Ministerial Meeting, from the Nanjing Statement at the APEC Human Resources Development Ministerial Meeting to 2026 APEC Leaders' Shenzhen Outlook at the Economic Leaders' Meeting, China placed economic and trade cooperation, innovation and people's livelihoods at the heart of its year-long APEC agenda. A total of 321 meetings and events and 75 major deliverables have provided more concrete avenues for Asia-Pacific cooperation, injecting fresh vitality and strong momentum into regional development. Some foreign media outlets have noted that, against a backdrop of mounting global geopolitical tensions, the Shenzhen meeting was one of the "few forums" capable of bringing "together" economies of different sizes. These achievements reflect the host's year-long commitment and demonstrate that, by identifying common interests, economies can continue to unleash the vitality and potential of the Asia-Pacific economy and advance the building of an Asia-Pacific community. Many leaders and foreign media outlets have praised Shenzhen, remarking that every time they come, it looks different. Shenzhen itself also offers the world a glimpse of how China is advancing high-standard opening-up. Having grown amid China's reform and opening-up, Shenzhen has now become a key node in global industrial chains and innovation networks. By hosting the APEC meeting in Shenzhen and announcing new funding for APEC practical cooperation to launch new cooperation institutions covering digital technology, cross-border data flow, clean energy, and the development of SMEs, China shows its sincerity in committing resources and sharing development opportunities. Asia-Pacific economies vary widely in their stages of development. Some prioritize market access, while others are in urgent need of infrastructure and talent. China brings these diverse needs into a single cooperation agenda, enabling all parties to find pathways for participation. This vision carries substantial practical weight. The trust that Asia-Pacific partners place in China also stems from China's strategic resolve to take root in the Asia-Pacific, contribute to its development and deliver benefits to the region. China outlined the way forward in Shenzhen, facilitated agreement among all parties on concrete actions, and readied resources and platforms to implement those actions. These efforts have shown all parties that China is willing to listen to the concerns of different economies, has the ability to coordinate their respective interests, and demonstrates a sense of responsibility in advancing shared goals. Against narratives that frame economic ties as burdens and interdependence as risks, China continues to expand openness for the long-term interests of the entire Asia-Pacific. The dynamism of the Asia-Pacific economy stems from decades of close exchanges between people and enterprises. To preserve these connections is to safeguard shared opportunities for growth. Further recognition of the Shenzhen APEC meeting will translate into easier trade, smoother exchanges and broader access to innovative opportunities ahead. The gratitude expressed to China by participants in Shenzhen grows out of trust built through cooperation. China's actions over the year demonstrate that the more complex the international landscape becomes, the more the Asia-Pacific can find a sincere, reliable and capable leader on the path of open cooperation.

item.title: Time for Takaichi to retract her erroneous 'survival-threatening situation' remarks
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-20 12:35:00
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi speaks to reporters ahead of her departure for a tour of Europe at the Prime Minister's Official Residence in Tokyo on June 13, 2026. Photo: VCG On November 19, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi held a press conference after attending the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, reiterating that Japan's basic position on the Taiwan question remains consistent with the 1972 Sino-Japanese Joint Statement and emphasizing that "there has been absolutely no change to this position." She also said that "China is an important neighboring country," that the status of the four political documents as the "basic documents on Japan-China relations" remains unchanged, and that Japan is willing to comprehensively advance a strategic relationship of mutual benefit through dialogue and build "constructive and stable" China-Japan relations. However, when asked about with her erroneous remarks a year earlier that the Chinese mainland's "use of force on Taiwan" could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan, Takaichi continued to evade the question, saying that "she could not comment on hypothetical scenarios." The core principles of the Sino-Japanese Joint Statement are clearly set out in black and white: The Government of Japan recognizes that the Government of the People's Republic of China as the sole legal Government of China. The Government of the People's Republic of China reiterates that Taiwan is an inalienable part of the territory of the People's Republic of China. The Government of Japan fully understands and respects this stand of the Government of the People's Republic of China, and it firmly maintains its stand under Article 8 of the Postdam Proclamation. This statement, together with the other four political documents, including the Treaty of Peace and Friendship between China and Japan, forms the political foundation for the normalization of diplomatic relations between the two countries. These are commitments that both countries must uphold in their bilateral relations and an important part of the postwar international order. Linking a "contingency in Taiwan" to a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan and implying that Japan might exercise its right to collective self-defense directly undermines the framework established by the 1972 Sino-Japanese Joint Statement and seriously deviates from the postwar international order that Japan, as a defeated nation in World War II, is obliged to observe. If Japan's position on the Taiwan question is truly consistent with the Sino-Japan Joint Statement, it should acknowledge its mistake and publicly retract the provocative claim that "a Taiwan contingency is a Japan contingency." On the same day, the leaders of China, Russia and the US held a historic trilateral meeting in Shenzhen and issued the China-Russia-US Heads of State Declaration toward Peace. All three leaders recalled the history of their countries fighting side by side during World War II, sending an important signal of their shared commitment to safeguarding the postwar international order - a message that Tokyo should take note of. The core documents underpinning the postwar international order include the Cairo Declaration and the Potsdam Proclamation, which made clear that Japan must return the Chinese territories it had seized, including Taiwan. Japan accepted the Potsdam Proclamation and surrendered unconditionally, and subsequently reaffirmed its commitment to adhering to Article 8 of the proclamation in the Sino-Japan Joint Statement. Any remarks that directly link the Taiwan question to Japan's security, or even imply possible military intervention, constitute an open challenge to the outcomes of the victory in World War II and the postwar international order. China-Japan relations remain strained over remarks concerning Taiwan, with tensions already affecting economic and trade ties, people-to-people exchanges and other areas. Takaichi has emphasized dialogue and a strategic relationship of mutual benefit, but her words must be matched by actions. If she sincerely wishes to improve China-Japan relations, retracting her erroneous remarks should be the first step. Otherwise, merely repeating that Japan's "position remains unchanged" without making substantive corrections will do little to inspire confidence or benefit Japan itself, or contribute to lasting peace and stability in the region.
